claim: Zika virus was discovered in Uganda in 1947.
source: Zika virus was discovered in Uganda in 1947 and is transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, which also act as vectors for dengue and chikungunya viruses throughout much of the tropical world.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dick et al., 1952 and Dick, 1953 in the Introduction section.

claim: Zika virus is transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes.
source: Zika virus was discovered in Uganda in 1947 and is transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, which also act as vectors for dengue and chikungunya viruses throughout much of the tropical world.
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Aedes mosquitoes act as vectors for dengue and chikungunya viruses throughout much of the tropical world.
source: Zika virus was discovered in Uganda in 1947 and is transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, which also act as vectors for dengue and chikungunya viruses throughout much of the tropical world.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Aedes mosquitoes.

claim: In 2007, a Zika virus outbreak in the Federated States of Micronesia sparked public health concern.
source: In 2007, an outbreak in the Federated States of Micronesia sparked public health concern.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lanciotti et al., 2008 in the Introduction.

claim: In 2013, Zika virus began to spread across parts of Oceania.
source: In 2013, the virus began to spread across other parts of Oceania and in 2015, a large outbreak in Latin America began in Brazil.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations in the Introduction section.

claim: In 2015, a large Zika virus outbreak in Latin America began in Brazil.
source: In 2013, the virus began to spread across other parts of Oceania and in 2015, a large outbreak in Latin America began in Brazil.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zanluca et al., 2015 and World Health Organisation, 2015.

claim: Possible associations with microcephaly and Guillain-Barré syndrome were observed in the 2015 Zika outbreak.
source: Possible associations with microcephaly and Guillain-Barré syndrome observed in this outbreak have raised concerns about continued global spread of Zika virus, prompting its declaration as a Public Health Emergency of International Concern by the World Health Organization.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to World Health Organisation, 2015 and Martines et al., 2016.

claim: Zika virus was declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern by the World Health Organization.
source: Possible associations with microcephaly and Guillain-Barré syndrome observed in this outbreak have raised concerns about continued global spread of Zika virus, prompting its declaration as a Public Health Emergency of International Concern by the World Health Organization.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to World Health Organisation and reference to Heymann et al., 2016.

claim: Over 2.17 billion people inhabit areas with suitable environmental conditions for Zika virus transmission.
source: We show a large portion of tropical and sub-tropical regions globally have suitable environmental conditions with over 2.17 billion people inhabiting these areas.
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis combining the environmental suitability map with population data.

claim: Zika virus is an emerging arbovirus carried by mosquitoes of the genus Aedes.
source: Zika virus (ZIKV) is an emerging arbovirus carried by mosquitoes of the genus Aedes (Musso et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Musso et al., 2014.

claim: Zika virus was only known to cause sporadic infections in humans in Africa and Asia until 2007.
source: Although discovered in Uganda in 1947 (Dick et al., 1952; Dick, 1953) ZIKV was only known to cause sporadic infections in humans in Africa and Asia until 2007 (Lanciotti et al., 2008), when it caused a large outbreak of symptomatic cases on Yap island in the Federated States of Micronesia (FSM), followed by another in French Polynesia in 2013–14 and subsequent spread across Oceania (Musso et al., 2015a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dick et al., 1952; Dick, 1953; and Lanciotti et al., 2008.

claim: Zika virus caused a large outbreak of symptomatic cases on Yap island in the Federated States of Micronesia in 2007.
source: Although discovered in Uganda in 1947 (Dick et al., 1952; Dick, 1953) ZIKV was only known to cause sporadic infections in humans in Africa and Asia until 2007 (Lanciotti et al., 2008), when it caused a large outbreak of symptomatic cases on Yap island in the Federated States of Micronesia (FSM), followed by another in French Polynesia in 2013–14 and subsequent spread across Oceania (Musso et al., 2015a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lanciotti et al., 2008.

claim: Zika virus caused an outbreak in French Polynesia in 2013-14.
source: Although discovered in Uganda in 1947 (Dick et al., 1952; Dick, 1953) ZIKV was only known to cause sporadic infections in humans in Africa and Asia until 2007 (Lanciotti et al., 2008), when it caused a large outbreak of symptomatic cases on Yap island in the Federated States of Micronesia (FSM), followed by another in French Polynesia in 2013–14 and subsequent spread across Oceania (Musso et al., 2015a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Musso et al., 2015a.

claim: In the 2007 Yap island outbreak, approximately 20% of ZIKV cases were symptomatic.
source: In the 2007 Yap island outbreak, it was estimated that approximately 20% of ZIKV cases were symptomatic.
evidence: The claim is stated as an estimate from the outbreak.

claim: Indigenous transmission of ZIKV to humans was reported for the first time in Latin America in 2015.
source: While indigenous transmission of ZIKV to humans was reported for the first time in Latin America in 2015 (Zanluca et al., 2015; World Health Organisation, 2015), recent phylogeographic research estimates that the virus was introduced into the region between May and December 2013 (Faria et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zanluca et al., 2015 and World Health Organisation, 2015.

claim: Phylogeographic research estimates that Zika virus was introduced into Latin America between May and December 2013.
source: While indigenous transmission of ZIKV to humans was reported for the first time in Latin America in 2015 (Zanluca et al., 2015; World Health Organisation, 2015), recent phylogeographic research estimates that the virus was introduced into the region between May and December 2013 (Faria et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Faria et al., 2016.

claim: The recent rapid spread of Zika virus has led to concern that it is following a similar pattern of global expansion to dengue and chikungunya.
source: This recent rapid spread has led to concern that the virus is following a similar pattern of global expansion to that of dengue and chikungunya (Musso et al., 2015a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Musso et al., 2015a.

claim: ZIKV has been isolated from 19 different Aedes species.
source: ZIKV has been isolated from 19 different Aedes species (Haddow et al., 2012; Grard et al., 2014), but virus has been most frequently found in Ae. aegypti (Monlun et al., 1992; Marchette et al., 1969; Smithburn, 1954; Pond, 1963; Faye et al., 2008; Foy et al., 2011b; WHO Collaborating Center for Reference and Research on Arboviruses and Hemorrhagic Fever Viruses: Annual Report, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Haddow et al., 2012 and Grard et al., 2014.

claim: Zika virus has been most frequently found in Ae. aegypti.
source: ZIKV has been isolated from 19 different Aedes species (Haddow et al., 2012; Grard et al., 2014), but virus has been most frequently found in Ae. aegypti (Monlun et al., 1992; Marchette et al., 1969; Smithburn, 1954; Pond, 1963; Faye et al., 2008; Foy et al., 2011b; WHO Collaborating Center for Reference and Research on Arboviruses and Hemorrhagic Fever Viruses: Annual Report, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations including Monlun et al., 1992; Marchette et al., 1969; Smithburn, 1954; Pond, 1963; Faye et al., 2008; Foy et al., 2011b.

claim: The current rapid spread of ZIKV in Latin America is indicative of Ae. aegypti as a highly efficient arbovirus vector.
source: These studies were based upon ancestral African strains of ZIKV, but the current rapid spread of ZIKV in Latin America is indicative of this highly efficient arbovirus vector (Marcondes and Ximenes, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Marcondes and Ximenes, 2015 and inference from observed spread patterns.

claim: The relatively recent global spread of Ae. albopictus may partially explain the lower frequency of ZIKV isolations from this species.
source: The relatively recent global spread of Ae. albopictus (Benedict et al., 2007; Kraemer et al., 2015c) and the rarity of ZIKV isolations from wild mosquitoes may also partially explain the lower frequency of isolations from Ae. albopictus populations.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from citations to Benedict et al., 2007 and Kraemer et al., 2015c.

claim: Virus transmission by Ae. albopictus and other minor vector species has normally resulted in only a small number of cases.
source: Whilst virus transmission by Ae. albopictus and other minor vector species has normally resulted in only a small number of cases (Kutsuna et al., 2015; Roiz et al., 2015), these vectors do pose the threat of limited transmission (Grard et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kutsuna et al., 2015 and Roiz et al., 2015.

claim: The wide geographic distribution of Ae. albopictus combined with frequent virus introduction via viraemic travellers means the risk for ZIKV infection via this vector must be considered in ZIKV mapping.
source: The wide geographic distribution of Ae. albopictus combined with the frequent virus introduction via viraemic travellers (McCarthy 2016; Bogoch et al., 2016; Morrison et al., 2008; Scott and Takken, 2012), means the risk for ZIKV infection via this vector must therefore also be considered in ZIKV mapping.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from citations about Ae. albopictus distribution and traveller-mediated virus introduction.

claim: ZIKV reporting was limited to a few small areas in Africa and Asia until 2007.
source: The fact that ZIKV reporting was limited to a few small areas in Africa and Asia until 2007 means that global risk mapping has not, until recently, been a priority (Pigott et al., 2015b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pigott et al., 2015b.

claim: Recent associations with Guillain-Barré syndrome in adults have revealed that ZIKV could lead to more severe complications than mild symptoms.
source: Recent associations with Guillain-Barré syndrome in adults and microcephaly in infants born to ZIKV-infected mothers (World Health Organisation, 2015; Martines et al., 2016) have revealed that ZIKV could lead to more severe complications than the mild rash and flu-like symptoms that characterize the majority of symptomatic cases (Gatherer and Kohl, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to World Health Organisation, 2015; Martines et al., 2016; and Gatherer and Kohl, 2016.

claim: Recent associations with microcephaly in infants born to ZIKV-infected mothers have revealed that ZIKV could lead to more severe complications than mild symptoms.
source: Recent associations with Guillain-Barré syndrome in adults and microcephaly in infants born to ZIKV-infected mothers (World Health Organisation, 2015; Martines et al., 2016) have revealed that ZIKV could lead to more severe complications than the mild rash and flu-like symptoms that characterize the majority of symptomatic cases (Gatherer and Kohl, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to World Health Organisation, 2015; Martines et al., 2016; and Gatherer and Kohl, 2016.

claim: The majority of symptomatic ZIKV cases are characterized by mild rash and flu-like symptoms.
source: Recent associations with Guillain-Barré syndrome in adults and microcephaly in infants born to ZIKV-infected mothers (World Health Organisation, 2015; Martines et al., 2016) have revealed that ZIKV could lead to more severe complications than the mild rash and flu-like symptoms that characterize the majority of symptomatic cases (Gatherer and Kohl, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gatherer and Kohl, 2016.

claim: There is potential for antigen-based diagnostic tests to exhibit cross-reactivity when IgM ELISA is used for rapid diagnosis of ZIKV.
source: Being a closely related flavivirus to DENV, there is furthermore the potential for antigen-based diagnostic tests to exhibit cross-reactivity when IgM ELISA is used for rapid diagnosis.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge about flavivirus relationships and diagnostic test characteristics.

claim: Currently the only method of confirming ZIKV infection is by using PCR on acute specimens.
source: Although ZIKV-specific serologic assays are being developed by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control, currently the only method of confirming ZIKV infection is by using PCR on acute specimens (Lanciotti et al., 2008, Faye et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lanciotti et al., 2008 and Faye et al., 2008.

claim: Species distribution modelling techniques have been useful for mapping dengue.
source: In this paper, we use species distribution modelling techniques that have been useful for mapping other vector-borne diseases such as dengue (Bhatt et al., 2013), Leishmaniasis (Pigott et al., 2014b), and Crimean-Congo Haemorrhagic Fever (Messina et al., 2015b) to map environmental suitability for ZIKV.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bhatt et al., 2013.

claim: Species distribution modelling techniques have been useful for mapping Leishmaniasis.
source: In this paper, we use species distribution modelling techniques that have been useful for mapping other vector-borne diseases such as dengue (Bhatt et al., 2013), Leishmaniasis (Pigott et al., 2014b), and Crimean-Congo Haemorrhagic Fever (Messina et al., 2015b) to map environmental suitability for ZIKV.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pigott et al., 2014b.

claim: Species distribution modelling techniques have been useful for mapping Crimean-Congo Haemorrhagic Fever.
source: In this paper, we use species distribution modelling techniques that have been useful for mapping other vector-borne diseases such as dengue (Bhatt et al., 2013), Leishmaniasis (Pigott et al., 2014b), and Crimean-Congo Haemorrhagic Fever (Messina et al., 2015b) to map environmental suitability for ZIKV.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Messina et al., 2015b.

claim: The environmental niche of a disease can be identified according to a combination of environmental conditions supporting its presence in a particular location.
source: The environmental niche of a disease can be identified according to a combination of environmental conditions supporting its presence in a particular location, with statistical modelling then allowing this niche to be described quantitatively (Kraemer et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kraemer et al., 2016.

claim: Niche modelling uses records of known disease occurrence alongside hypothesized environmental covariates to predict suitability for disease transmission in regions where it has yet to be reported.
source: Niche modelling uses records of known disease occurrence alongside hypothesized environmental covariates to predict suitability for disease transmission in regions where it has yet to be reported (Elith and Leathwick, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Elith and Leathwick, 2009.

claim: The final dataset contains 323 standardized occurrence records.
source: Figure 1A shows the locations of the 323 standardized occurrence records in the final dataset, classified by the following date ranges: (i) up until 2006 (before the outbreak in FSM); (ii) between 2007 (the year of the FSM outbreak) and 2014; and (iii) since 2015, the first reporting of ZIKV in the Americas.
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 63% of occurrences in the dataset come from the recent 2015-2016 outbreak in Latin America.
source: These figures highlight the more sporadic nature of reporting until recent years, with the majority of occurrences in the dataset (63%) coming from the recent 2015–2016 outbreak in Latin America.
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The final map resulted from the mean of 300 ensemble Boosted Regression Tree (BRT) models.
source: The final map that resulted from the mean of 300 ensemble Boosted Regression Tree (BRT) models is shown in Figure 2A (with greater detail shown for each region in Figures 2B–D).
evidence: The claim describes the methodology used to generate the results.

claim: Models were restricted to make predictions only within areas where mosquito vectors (Ae. aegypti) were able to persist.
source: We restricted our models to make predictions only within areas where i) mosquito vectors (in this case Ae. aegypti) were able to persist and ii) where temperature was sufficient for arboviral replication within the mosquito.
evidence: The claim describes a methodological constraint applied to the models.

claim: Models were restricted to make predictions only where temperature was sufficient for arboviral replication within the mosquito.
source: We restricted our models to make predictions only within areas where i) mosquito vectors (in this case Ae. aegypti) were able to persist and ii) where temperature was sufficient for arboviral replication within the mosquito.
evidence: The claim describes a methodological constraint applied to the models.

claim: Large portions of the Americas are suitable for ZIKV transmission.
source: Our models predicted high levels of risk for ZIKV in many areas within the tropical and sub-tropical zones. Large portions of the Americas are suitable for transmission, with the largest areas of risk occurring in Brazil, followed by Colombia and Venezuela, all of which have reported high numbers of cases in the 2015–2016 outbreak.
evidence: The claim is based on model predictions presented in the manuscript.

claim: The largest areas of risk in the Americas occur in Brazil, followed by Colombia and Venezuela.
source: Large portions of the Americas are suitable for transmission, with the largest areas of risk occurring in Brazil, followed by Colombia and Venezuela, all of which have reported high numbers of cases in the 2015–2016 outbreak.
evidence: The claim is based on model predictions presented in the manuscript.

claim: In Brazil, the coastal cities in the south and large areas of the north have the highest environmental suitability for ZIKV.
source: In Brazil, where the highest numbers of ZIKV are reported in the ongoing epidemic, the coastal cities in the south as well as large areas of the north are identified to have the highest environmental suitability of ZIKV.
evidence: The claim is based on model predictions presented in the manuscript.

claim: The central region of Brazil has low population densities and smaller mosquito populations.
source: The central region of Brazil, on the other hand, has low population densities and smaller mosquito populations, which is reflected in the relatively low suitability for ZIKV transmission seen in the map.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from population and mosquito distribution data.

claim: A large portion of the southeast region of the USA, including much of Texas through to Florida, is highly suitable for ZIKV transmission.
source: Although ZIKV has yet to be reported in the USA, a large portion of the southeast region of the country, including much of Texas through to Florida, is also highly suitable for transmission.
evidence: The claim is based on model predictions presented in the manuscript.

claim: Potential risk for ZIKV transmission is high in much of sub-Saharan Africa.
source: Potential risk for ZIKV transmission is high in much of sub-Saharan Africa, with continuous suitability in the Democratic Republic of Congo and surrounding areas and several sporadic case reports in western sub-Saharan countries since the 1950s.
evidence: The claim is based on model predictions presented in the manuscript.

claim: Over 2 million square kilometres of India is at potential risk for ZIKV transmission.
source: Although no symptomatic cases have yet been reported in India, a large portion of this country is at potential risk for ZIKV transmission (over 2 million square kilometres), with environmental suitability extending from its northwest regions through to Bangladesh and Myanmar.
evidence: The claim is based on model predictions and area calculations presented in the manuscript.

claim: The area suitable for ZIKV transmission in Australia's northernmost regions comprises nearly 250,000 square kilometres.
source: While only representing less than ten percent of Australia's total land area, the area shown to be suitable for ZIKV transmission in its northernmost regions is considerable (comprising nearly 250,000 square kilometres).
evidence: The claim is based on model predictions and area calculations presented in the manuscript.

claim: ZIKV risk is particularly influenced by annual cumulative precipitation, contributing 65.0% to the variation in the ensemble of models.
source: Our models showed ZIKV risk to be particularly influenced by annual cumulative precipitation, contributing 65.0% to the variation in the ensemble of models.
evidence: The claim is based on model analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Temperature suitability for DENV transmission via Ae. albopictus contributed 14.6% to model variation.
source: The next most important predictor in the model was temperature suitability for DENV transmission via Ae. albopictus, contributing 14.6%.
evidence: The claim is based on model analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Urban extents contributed 8.3% to model variation.
source: These are followed by urban extents (8.3%), temperature suitability for DENV via Ae. aegypti (5.7%), the Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI; 3.8%), and minimum relative humidity (2.5%).
evidence: The claim is based on model analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Temperature suitability for DENV via Ae. aegypti contributed 5.7% to model variation.
source: These are followed by urban extents (8.3%), temperature suitability for DENV via Ae. aegypti (5.7%), the Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI; 3.8%), and minimum relative humidity (2.5%).
evidence: The claim is based on model analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI) contributed 3.8% to model variation.
source: These are followed by urban extents (8.3%), temperature suitability for DENV via Ae. aegypti (5.7%), the Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI; 3.8%), and minimum relative humidity (2.5%).
evidence: The claim is based on model analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Minimum relative humidity contributed 2.5% to model variation.
source: These are followed by urban extents (8.3%), temperature suitability for DENV via Ae. aegypti (5.7%), the Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI; 3.8%), and minimum relative humidity (2.5%).
evidence: The claim is based on model analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Validation statistics indicated high predictive performance of the BRT ensemble mean map with area under the receiver operating characteristic (AUC) of 0.829 (± 0.121 SD).
source: Validation statistics indicated high predictive performance of the BRT ensemble mean map evaluated in a 10-fold cross-validation procedure, with area under the receiver operating characteristic (AUC) of 0.829 ( ± 0.121 SD).
evidence: The claim is based on validation analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: A threshold environmental suitability value of 0.397 was determined to incorporate 90% of all ZIKV occurrence locations.
source: A threshold environmental suitability value of 0.397 in our final map was determined to incorporate 90% of all ZIKV occurrence locations.
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: 2.17 billion people globally live within areas that are environmentally suitable for ZIKV transmission.
source: Using high-resolution global population estimates (WorldPop, 2015; SEDAC, 2015), we summed the populations living in Zika-suitable areas and have identified 2.17 billion people globally living within areas that are environmentally suitable for ZIKV transmission.
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis combining suitability maps with population data.

claim: Asia has 1.42 billion people living in areas suitable for ZIKV transmission.
source: Asia has the most people living in areas that are suitable for ZIKV transmission at 1.42 billion, accounted for in large part by those living in India.
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis presented in Table 1.

claim: In Africa, roughly 453 million people are living in areas suitable for ZIKV transmission.
source: In Africa, roughly 453 million people are living in areas suitable for ZIKV transmission, the largest proportion of which live in Nigeria.
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis presented in Table 1.

claim: In the Americas, more than 298 million people live in ZIKV-suitable transmission zones.
source: In the Americas, more than 298 million people live in ZIKV-suitable transmission zones, with approximately 40 percent of these people living in Brazil.
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis presented in Table 1.

claim: Approximately 40 percent of people living in ZIKV-suitable transmission zones in the Americas live in Brazil.
source: In the Americas, more than 298 million people live in ZIKV-suitable transmission zones, with approximately 40 percent of these people living in Brazil.
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Within the majority of environmentally suitable areas for ZIKV in the Americas, prolonged year-round transmission is possible.
source: Within the majority of environmentally suitable areas for ZIKV in the Americas, prolonged year-round transmission is possible.
evidence: The claim is based on model predictions presented in the manuscript.

claim: 5.42 million births will occur in the Americas over the next year within areas and times of environmental suitability for ZIKV transmission.
source: Using high-resolution data on births for the year 2015 (WorldPop, 2015), we also estimate that 5.42 million births will occur in the Americas over the next year within areas and times of environmental suitability for ZIKV transmission.
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis combining suitability maps with birth data.

claim: Of the 53 species of Flavivirus, 19 are reported to have caused illness in humans.
source: Of the 53 species of Flavivirus, 19 are reported to have caused illness in humans (ICTV, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to ICTV, 2014.

claim: Approximately 219 viruses are known to be pathogenic.
source: A large number of viruses (circa 219) are known to be pathogenic (Woolhouse et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Woolhouse et al., 2012.

claim: Environmental suitability for virus transmission in an area does not necessarily mean that it will arrive and/or establish in that location.
source: Environmental suitability for virus transmission in an area does not necessarily mean that it will arrive and/or establish in that location.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference about the limitations of environmental suitability models.

claim: Arboviral infections are dependent on human mobility from travel, trade, and migration, which introduce viruses to places where mosquito vectors are already present.
source: Arboviral infections in particular are dependent on a variety of non-environmental factors, with their movement having historically been largely attributed to human mobility from travel, trade, and migration, which introduce the viruses to places where mosquito vectors are already present (Murray et al., 2013; Weaver and Reisen, 2010; Nunes et al., 2015; Gubler and Clark, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Murray et al., 2013; Weaver and Reisen, 2010; Nunes et al., 2015; Gubler and Clark, 1995.

claim: Importation of ZIKV could give rise to subsequent autochthonous cases in locations with permissible environments for transmission.
source: The identification of locations with permissible environments for transmission of emerging diseases like ZIKV is crucial, as importation could give rise to subsequent autochthonous cases in these locations (Hennessey et al., 2016; Zanluca et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hennessey et al., 2016 and Zanluca et al., 2015.

claim: How the ongoing epidemic unfolds in terms of case numbers will depend on local transmission dynamics, herd immunity, patterns of contact among mosquitoes and infectious and susceptible humans, and mosquito-to-human ratios.
source: How the ongoing epidemic unfolds in terms of case numbers (or incidence) will depend on a range of other factors such as local transmission dynamics, herd immunity, patterns of contact among mosquitoes and infectious and susceptible humans (Stoddard et al., 2013), and mosquito-to-human ratios as recently shown for dengue (Kraemer et al., 2015a) and chikungunya (Salje et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Stoddard et al., 2013; Kraemer et al., 2015a; and Salje et al., 2016.

claim: Not all individuals in suitable areas will be exposed to ZIKV.
source: It is important to recognize that not all individuals will be exposed to ZIKV.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference about disease transmission dynamics.

claim: A ZIKV outbreak may be temporally and spatially sporadic even in the most receptive environments.
source: Like with other flaviviruses, a ZIKV outbreak may be temporally and spatially sporadic and, even in the most receptive environments, is unlikely that all of the population will be infected.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge about flavivirus transmission patterns.

claim: Increasing herd immunity of ZIKV will rapidly reduce the size of the susceptible population at risk for infection in subsequent years.
source: Furthermore, increasing herd immunity of this likely sterilizing infection will rapidly reduce the size of the susceptible population at risk for infection in subsequent years (Dick et al., 1952) and work is ongoing to predict the likely infection dynamics after establishment.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dick et al., 1952 and inference about immunity dynamics.

claim: Public health education about reducing populations and avoiding contact with mosquito vectors is required in at-risk areas for all arboviral diseases.
source: For all arboviral diseases, public health education about reducing populations and avoiding contact with mosquito vectors is required in at-risk areas.
evidence: The claim is based on established public health knowledge.

claim: Public health agencies have issued warnings for women who are currently or planning on becoming pregnant in areas suspected to have ongoing ZIKV transmission.
source: Specific to ZIKV is the risk of microcephaly in newborns, which has led public health agencies to issue warnings for women who are currently or planning on becoming pregnant in areas suspected to have ongoing ZIKV transmission and the declaration of a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (Heymann et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Heymann et al., 2016.

claim: Instances of ZIKV sexual transmission have been reported.
source: It should be noted that instances of ZIKV sexual transmission have been reported (Patino-Barbosa et al., 2015; Musso et al., 2015b; Foy et al., 2011a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Patino-Barbosa et al., 2015; Musso et al., 2015b; Foy et al., 2011a.

claim: A great deal of basic epidemiological information specific to ZIKV is lacking.
source: A great deal of basic epidemiological information specific to ZIKV is lacking.
evidence: The claim is based on assessment of the current state of knowledge.

claim: Temperature suitability for dengue was entered into the models due to the greater number of field and laboratory studies available for parameterising this metric for DENV.
source: For this reason, temperature suitability for dengue (Brady et al., 2013, 2014) was entered into the models due to the greater number of field and laboratory studies available for parameterising this metric for DENV.
evidence: The claim explains a methodological choice based on available data.

claim: All covariates in the models could equally be applied to mapping DENV and CHIKV.
source: Indeed, all other covariates in our models could equally be applied to mapping DENV and CHIKV, and ZIKV-specific refinements to modelling covariates will be possible as the disease continues to expand to allow for improvements in future iterations of the map.
evidence: The claim is based on inference about the applicability of covariates to related diseases.

claim: The relatively smaller amount of occurrence data available for ZIKV (especially prior to recent outbreaks) means that this dataset should be updated with new information as necessary.
source: The relatively smaller amount of occurrence data available for ZIKV (especially prior to recent outbreaks) means that this dataset should also be updated with new information as necessary, leading to a stronger global evidence base and improved accuracy of future maps.
evidence: The claim is based on inference about data limitations and future improvements.

claim: The study produced the first global high spatial-resolution map of environmental suitability for ZIKV transmission to humans.
source: In this study, we produced the first global high spatial-resolution map of environmental suitability for ZIKV transmission to humans using an assembly of known records of ZIKV occurrence and environmental covariates in a species distribution modelling framework.
evidence: The claim describes the primary output of the study.

claim: Knowledge of the potential distribution can encourage more vigilant surveillance in both humans and Aedes mosquito populations.
source: Knowledge of the potential distribution can encourage more vigilant surveillance in both humans and Aedes mosquito populations, as well as help in the allocation of limited resources for disease prevention.
evidence: The claim is based on inference about the utility of the mapping results.

claim: The maps and underlying data are freely available online via figshare.
source: The maps and underlying data are freely available online via figshare (http://www.figshare.com).
evidence: The claim states a fact about data availability.

claim: The study applied a species distribution modelling approach to establish a multivariate empirical relationship between the probability of ZIKV occurrence and environmental conditions.
source: To map environmental suitability for ZIKV transmission to humans, we applied a species distribution modelling approach to establish a multivariate empirical relationship between the probability of ZIKV occurrence and the environmental conditions in locations where the disease has been confirmed.
evidence: The claim describes the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: The study employed an ensemble boosted regression trees (BRT) methodology.
source: We employed an ensemble boosted regression trees (BRT) methodology (De'ath, 2007; Elith et al., 2008), which required the generation of: (i) a comprehensive compendium of known locations of disease occurrence in humans; (ii) a set of background points representing locations where ZIKV has not yet been reported; and (iii) a set of high-resolution globally gridded environmental and socioeconomic covariates hypothesised to affect ZIKV transmission.
evidence: The claim describes the methodological approach with supporting citations to De'ath, 2007 and Elith et al., 2008.

claim: The resulting model produces a 5 x 5 km spatial-resolution global map of environmental suitability for ZIKV transmission to humans.
source: The resulting model produces a 5 x 5 km spatial-resolution global map of environmental suitability for ZIKV transmission to humans.
evidence: The claim describes the output of the modeling approach.

claim: Information about the locations of ZIKV occurrence in humans was extracted from peer-reviewed literature, case reports, and informal online sources.
source: Information about the locations of ZIKV occurrence in humans was extracted from peer-reviewed literature, case reports, and informal online sources following previously established protocols (Kraemer et al., 2015b; Messina et al., 2014; 2015a).
evidence: The claim describes the data collection methodology with supporting citations.

claim: Literature searches were undertaken using PubMed and ISI Web of Science search engines using the search term 'Zika'.
source: To collate the peer-reviewed dataset, literature searches were undertaken using PubMed (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed) and ISI Web of Science (http://www.webofknowledge.com) search engines using the search term 'Zika'.
evidence: The claim describes the literature search methodology.

claim: The literature search resulted in the review of 148 references ranging in publication dates between 1951 and 2015.
source: No language restrictions were placed on these searches; however, only those citations with a full title and abstract were retrieved, resulting in the review of 148 references ranging in publication dates between 1951 and 2015.
evidence: The claim describes the scope of the literature review.

claim: ProMED-mail was searched using the term 'Zika', resulting in the review of 139 reports between 27 June 2007 and 18 January 2016.
source: ProMED-mail (http://www.promedmail.org) was also searched using the term 'Zika', resulting in the review of 139 reports between 27 June 2007 and 18 January 2016.
evidence: The claim describes the ProMED-mail search results.

claim: Only laboratory confirmation of symptomatic ZIKV infection in humans was entered into the dataset.
source: From all sources, only laboratory confirmation of symptomatic ZIKV infection in humans was entered into the dataset (mention of suspected cases was not entered).
evidence: The claim describes an inclusion criterion for the dataset.

claim: Serological evidence from healthy individuals could represent a past infection with transmission potentially occurring in a different location.
source: Serological evidence from healthy individuals could represent a past infection, with transmission potentially occurring in a different location to that where the individual currently resides (Darwish et al., 1983), or could be an artefact from possible cross-reactivity with a variety of different viruses (Smithburn et al., 1954).
evidence: The claim is based on inference supported by citations to Darwish et al., 1983 and Smithburn et al., 1954.

claim: Usable location information was extracted from 110 sources.
source: In total, usable location information was extracted from 110 sources.
evidence: The claim describes the number of sources used for data extraction.

claim: An occurrence was defined as a unique location with one or more confirmed cases of ZIKV occurring within one calendar year.
source: Due to the potential for multiple independent reports referring to the same cases temporal and spatial standardization was required, as we have described previously in detail for dengue mapping efforts (Messina et al., 2014). In brief, an occurrence was defined as a unique location with one or more confirmed cases of ZIKV occurring within one calendar year (the finest temporal resolution available across all records).
evidence: The claim describes the definition used for data standardization.

claim: All polygons whose geographic area was greater than one square decimal degree were removed from the dataset.
source: Furthermore, all polygons whose geographic area was greater than one square decimal degree (approximately 111 square kilometers at the equator) were removed from the dataset to avoid averaging covariate values over very large areas, and only those occurrences comprising symptomatic individuals were retained for modelling purposes to ensure an accurate location of infection.
evidence: The claim describes an exclusion criterion for the dataset.

claim: The final occurrence dataset contained 323 unique occurrences.
source: In total, the final occurrence dataset contained 323 unique occurrences to be entered into our BRT modelling procedure.
evidence: The claim describes the size of the final dataset.

claim: 10,000 background locations were drawn using a biased sample based on the inverse of the combined-Aedes occurrence probability layer.
source: The inverse of this combined-Aedes occurrence probability layer (higher values indicating greater certainty of absence) was then used to draw a biased sample of 10,000 background locations.
evidence: The claim describes the methodology for generating background locations.

claim: The background locations were weighted such that their total sum was equal to the total number of occurrence locations (n=237; pseudo-absence weighting=0.0237).
source: These 10,000 background locations were combined with the standardized occurrence dataset to serve as comparison data locations in the BRT species distribution modelling procedure. The background locations were weighted such that their total sum was equal to the total number of occurrence locations (n=237; pseudo-absence weighting=0.0237), in order to aid in the discrimination capacity of the model (Barbet-Massin et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim describes the weighting methodology with supporting citation to Barbet-Massin et al., 2012.

claim: Six covariates hypothesized to influence the global distribution of ZIKV transmission to humans were used in the models.
source: A set of six covariates hypothesized to influence the global distribution of ZIKV transmission to humans were used in our models to establish an empirical relationship between ZIKV presence or absence and underlying environmental conditions.
evidence: The claim describes the number of covariates used in the models.

claim: Temperature affects key physiological processes in Aedes mosquitoes, including age- and temperature-dependent adult female survival and the duration of the extrinsic incubation period (EIP) of arboviruses.
source: Temperature affects key physiological processes in Aedes mosquitoes, including age- and temperature-dependent adult female survival, as well as the duration of the extrinsic incubation period (EIP) of arboviruses and the length of the gonotrophic cycle (Brady et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Brady et al., 2013.

claim: Temperature data was obtained from WorldClim v1.03, which uses historic global meteorological station data from 1961-2005 to interpolate global climate surfaces.
source: We obtained temperature data from WorldClim v1.03 (http://www.wordclim.org), which uses historic global meteorological station data from 1961–2005 to interpolate global climate surfaces.
evidence: The claim describes the source and characteristics of temperature data.

claim: MARKSIM software was used to apply the coefficients of 17 Global Climate Models (GCMs) to estimate temperature values for the year 2015.
source: MARKSIM software (Jones and Thornton, 2000) was then used to apply the coefficients of 17 Global Climate Models (GCMs) to estimate temperature values for the year 2015.
evidence: The claim describes the methodology for estimating 2015 temperature values with citation to Jones and Thornton, 2000.

claim: Presence of static surface water in natural or man-made containers is a pre-requisite for Aedes oviposition and larval and pupal development.
source: Presence of static surface water in natural or man-made containers is a pre-requisite for Aedes oviposition and larval and pupal development.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Aedes mosquito biology.

claim: Areas with greater amounts of precipitation are generally associated with higher DENV infection risk.
source: While fine-scale spatial and temporal heterogeneities have been observed between precipitation, vector abundance, and incidence of human DENV infections, there is evidence that areas with greater amounts of precipitation are generally associated with higher DENV infection risk (Chandy et al., 2013; Chowell and Sanchez, 2006; Dom et al., 2013; Pinto et al., 2011; Restrepo et al., 2014; Sang et al., 2014; Sankari et al., 2012; Campbell et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations including Chandy et al., 2013; Chowell and Sanchez, 2006; Dom et al., 2013; Pinto et al., 2011; Restrepo et al., 2014; Sang et al., 2014; Sankari et al., 2012; Campbell et al., 2015.

claim: Greater relative humidity has been found to promote DENV propagation in Ae. aegypti mosquitoes in several localized settings.
source: Greater relative humidity has been found to promote DENV propagation in Ae. aegypti mosquitoes in several localized settings (Colón-González et al., 2011; Thu et al., 1998), and has also been found to be an important contributor when predicting DENV risk at a global scale (Hales et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Colón-González et al., 2011; Thu et al., 1998; and Hales et al., 2002.

claim: A close association has been shown between local moisture supply, vegetation canopy development, and abundance of mosquito reproduction.
source: A close association has been shown between local moisture supply, vegetation canopy development, and abundance of mosquito reproduction (Linthicum et al., 1999), with previous studies highlighting the importance of moisture-related measures such as relative humidity to DENV occurrence (Hales et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Linthicum et al., 1999 and Hales et al., 2002.

claim: Both Aedes eggs and adults require moisture to survive.
source: Although resistant to desiccation, both Aedes eggs and adults require moisture to survive (Cox et al., 2007; Sota and Mogi, 1992; Reiskind and Lounibos, 2009; Costa et al., 2010; Luz et al., 2008), with low dry season moisture levels substantially affecting Aedes mortality (Russell et al., 2001; Trpis, 1972; Luz et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations including Cox et al., 2007; Sota and Mogi, 1992; Reiskind and Lounibos, 2009; Costa et al., 2010; Luz et al., 2008.

claim: Vegetation canopy cover has been associated with higher Aedes larvae density.
source: Vegetation canopy cover has previously been associated with higher Aedes larvae density (Fuller et al., 2009; Troyo et al., 2009; Bisset Lazcano et al., 2006; Barrera et al., 2006) by reducing evaporation from containers, decreasing sub-canopy wind speed, and protecting outdoor habitats from direct sunlight.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fuller et al., 2009; Troyo et al., 2009; Bisset Lazcano et al., 2006; Barrera et al., 2006.

claim: Ae. aegypti is found in close proximity to human dwellings often breeding in artificial containers.
source: There is a well-established link between urban areas, some vector borne diseases, and their vectors. In particular, Ae. aegypti is found in close proximity to human dwellings often breeding in artificial containers (Brown et al., 2011; Powell and Tabachnick, 2013; Kraemer et al., 2015c).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brown et al., 2011; Powell and Tabachnick, 2013; Kraemer et al., 2015c.

claim: The boosted regression tree (BRT) modelling procedure combines regression trees with gradient boosting.
source: The boosted regression tree (BRT) modelling procedure combines regression trees with gradient boosting (Friedman, 2001).
evidence: The claim describes the BRT methodology with citation to Friedman, 2001.

claim: BRT has been successfully employed in the past to map dengue and its Aedes mosquito vectors, as well as other vector-borne diseases.
source: As such, this approach has been successfully employed in the past to map dengue and its Aedes mosquito vectors, as well as other vector-borne diseases (Bhatt et al., 2013; Pigott et al., 2014b; Messina et al., 2015b; Kraemer et al., 2015c).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bhatt et al., 2013; Pigott et al., 2014b; Messina et al., 2015b; Kraemer et al., 2015c.

claim: An ensemble of 300 BRT models was fitted to separate bootstraps of the data to increase robustness and quantify model uncertainty.
source: To increase the robustness of model predictions and quantify model uncertainty, we fitted an ensemble (Araújo and New, 2007) of 300 BRT models to separate bootstraps of the data.
evidence: The claim describes the ensemble modeling approach with citation to Araújo and New, 2007.

claim: The central tendency was evaluated as the mean across all 300 BRT models.
source: We then evaluated the central tendency as the mean across all 300 BRT models (Bhatt et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim describes the method for calculating central tendency with citation to Bhatt et al., 2013.

claim: Each of the 300 models predicts environmental suitability on a continuous scale from 0 to 1.
source: Each of the 300 models predicts environmental suitability on a continuous scale from 0 to 1, with a final prediction map then being generated by calculating the mean prediction across all models for each 5 km x 5 km pixel.
evidence: The claim describes the output scale of the models.

claim: A pairwise distance sampling procedure was used to avoid AUC inflation due to spatial sorting bias.
source: Additionally, to avoid AUC inflation due to spatial sorting bias, a pairwise distance sampling procedure was used, resulting in a final AUC which is lower than would be returned by standard procedures but which gives a more realistic quantification of the model's ability to extrapolate predictions to new regions (Wenger and Olden, 2012).
evidence: The claim describes a methodological approach with citation to Wenger and Olden, 2012.

claim: Models were restricted to make predictions only within areas where Ae. aegypti probability of occurrence is more than 0.8 or temperature is conducive to transmission for at least 355 days in an average year.
source: We restricted our models to make predictions only within areas where either Ae. aegypti probability of occurrence (Kraemer et al., 2015c) is more than 0.8 or temperature is conducive to transmission for at least 355 days in an average year.
evidence: The claim describes the spatial restrictions applied to model predictions.

claim: A threshold cut-off of 90% was chosen to reflect potential errors or inaccurate locations in the occurrence point dataset.
source: To do this, we carried out a protocol previously used in (Pigott et al., 2015a), choosing a threshold environmental suitability value that encompasses 90% of the ZIKV occurrence point locations. This threshold cut-off of 90% was chosen (rather than 100%) to reflect potential errors or inaccurate locations in the occurrence point dataset.
evidence: The claim explains the rationale for the threshold choice with citation to Pigott et al., 2015a.

claim: The proportion of the year suitable for ZIKV transmission was derived from existing temperature suitability models.
source: This proportion was derived from existing temperature suitability models (Brady et al., 2013; 2014), which predict the total number of days within an average year that arbovirus transmission can be sustained in Ae. aegypti, assuming there is a local human reservoir of infection.
evidence: The claim describes the source of temporal suitability data with citations to Brady et al., 2013 and 2014.

claim: The limited information currently available on arboviruses suggests that their intra-mosquito viral dynamics are similar to dengue virus.
source: While the intra-mosquito viral dynamics in this model were parameterised for dengue virus, the limited information currently available on other arboviruses suggests that their dynamics are similar (Lambrechts et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lambrechts et al., 2011.
